# Overview



**Disobind** is a deep learning method that predicts **inter-protein contact maps** and **interface residues** for an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and its binding partner, using only their amino acid sequences. It addresses a critical gap in computational structural biology: while folded protein interactions are well-served by tools like AlphaFold2, disordered protein interactions—where one partner lacks a stable structure—remain exceptionally difficult to predict. Disobind fills this niche by leveraging protein language model embeddings (ProtT5) and a custom neural architecture (Epsilon_3) to infer *where* two proteins interact at residue-level resolution. When combined with AlphaFold2 structural predictions (the **Disobind+AF2** mode), it can further refine results by merging sequence-based and structure-based confidence signals.

![main_fig](https://github.com/isblab/disobind/blob/main/main.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L10), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L1-L14)

## What Disobind Predicts

Disobind operates on **binary protein complexes** (Protein A + Protein B) and produces two distinct prediction types, each available at multiple coarse-grained (CG) resolutions:

| Prediction Type | Description | Output Format | CG Resolutions |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Interaction (Contact Map)** | Which residue in Protein 1 contacts which residue in Protein 2 | `[L1 × L2]` matrix of contact probabilities | 1, 5, 10 |
| **Interface Residues** | Which residues in each protein participate in the interface | `[L1 + L2]` vector of interface probabilities | 1, 5, 10 |

At **CG-1**, each prediction corresponds to a single residue. At **CG-5** or **CG-10**, residues are grouped into "beads" of 5 or 10 residues, and predictions are averaged over each bead—this is useful for longer disordered regions where fine-grained prediction may be noisy. By default, Disobind runs interface prediction at CG-1 only, which is the highest-resolution setting.

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L130-L165), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L831-L890)

## Prediction Pipeline at a Glance

The end-to-end workflow—from raw protein identifiers to final residue-level predictions—follows a deterministic sequence of stages. Each stage is encapsulated within the `Disobind` class in `run_disobind.py`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input File<br/>(CSV or FASTA)"] --> B["Parse Protein Pairs<br/>Extract UniProt IDs & residue ranges"]
    B --> C["Download UniProt Sequences<br/>(parallelized via multiprocessing)"]
    C --> D["Generate ProtT5 Embeddings<br/>(1024-dim per residue)"]
    D --> E["Load Pre-trained Epsilon_3 Models<br/>(separate models per task & CG)"]
    E --> F["Run Neural Network Inference<br/>Projection → Interaction Tensor → Output"]
    F --> G{"AF2 Input Provided?"}
    G -- Yes --> H["Extract AF2 Confident Interactions<br/>(pLDDT > 70, PAE < 5, dist < 8Å)"]
    H --> I["Merge: Disobind+AF2<br/>(element-wise max)"]
    G -- No --> J["Output Disobind Predictions Only"]
    I --> K["Write CSV + .npy Outputs"]
    J --> K
```

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L111-L127), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L168-L207), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L667-L796)

## The Epsilon_3 Neural Architecture

All Disobind models share the **Epsilon_3** architecture—a purpose-built network that processes *pairs* of protein embeddings. The architecture decomposes into four sequential blocks:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Projection
        P1["Projection Layer 1<br/>Linear(1024→128) + ELU + LayerNorm"]
        P2["Projection Layer 2<br/>(separate or shared)"]
    end
    subgraph Interaction
        IT["Interaction Tensor<br/>outer-product-diff ⊕ outer-product-sum"]
        IB["Interface Block<br/>(masked avg2d pooling)"]
    end
    subgraph Hidden
        DS["Downsampling Layers"]
        US["Upsampling Layers"]
    end
    subgraph Output
        OL["Linear → Sigmoid<br/>(with optional temperature scaling)"]
    end
    P1 --> IT
    P2 --> IT
    IT --> IB
    IB --> DS
    DS --> US
    US --> OL
```

**Projection Block** — Each protein's 1024-dimensional ProtT5 per-residue embeddings are independently projected to a lower-dimensional space (128-dim by default) using a linear layer followed by ELU activation and LayerNorm. The two projection layers can be shared (tied weights) or separate.

**Interaction Tensor** — The projected embeddings `z1` and `z2` are combined into a 4D tensor `[N, L1, L2, 2C]` using two complementary outer-product operations (element-wise difference and element-wise sum), capturing both complementary and conserved interaction features between all residue pairs.

**Interface Block** — For interface prediction, the 4D interaction tensor is reduced via masked average-2d pooling along each protein axis, yielding interface probability vectors for both proteins simultaneously. For contact map prediction, the tensor is reshaped directly into a 2D contact matrix.

**Hidden & Output Blocks** — Optional downsampling/upsampling layers (with residual connections) process the features before a final linear projection and sigmoid activation produce per-residue (or per-bead) probabilities.

Sources: [src/models/Epsilon_3.py](/src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L15-L151), [src/models/Epsilon_3.py](/src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L155-L178), [src/models/Epsilon_3.py](/src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L267-L296), [src/models/get_layers.py](/src/models/get_layers.py#L17-L84)

## Model Versions and Configuration

Disobind ships with **six pre-trained model variants**, organized by prediction objective and coarse-grained resolution. Each variant is a distinct Epsilon_3 model with its own trained parameters:

| Model Version | Objective | CG Resolution | Config File | Key Difference |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Epsilon_3_6 | Interaction (contact map) | CG-10 | `Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.yml` | 3 downsampling layers, scale factor 2 |
| Epsilon_3_6.1 | Interaction | CG-5 | `Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.1.yml` | 3 downsampling layers, scale factor 2 |
| Epsilon_3_6.2 | Interaction | CG-1 | `Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.2.yml` | 3 downsampling layers, scale factor 2 |
| Epsilon_3_16 | Interface residues | CG-1 | `Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.yml` | No hidden layers (direct projection→output) |
| Epsilon_3_16.1 | Interface | CG-5 | `Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.1.yml` | No hidden layers |
| Epsilon_3_16.2 | Interface | CG-10 | `Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.2.yml` | No hidden layers |

The interaction models (Version 6.x) use downsampling layers to compress the feature space before upsampling back, while the interface models (Version 16.x) bypass hidden layers entirely—a simpler architecture that directly maps the interaction tensor to interface probabilities. All models use ProtT5 global embeddings, ELU activation, LayerNorm, and the AdamW optimizer with exponential learning rate scheduling.

> [!TIP]
> When invoking Disobind, the system automatically selects the correct model variant based on the requested objective and CG resolution—you never need to specify model versions manually. The mapping is defined in `analysis/params.py`.

Sources: [analysis/params.py](/analysis/params.py#L1-L59), [params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.yml](/params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.yml#L1-L57), [params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.yml](/params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.yml#L1-L58)

## Disobind and AlphaFold2 Integration

A distinctive capability of Disobind is its **Disobind+AF2** mode, which fuses sequence-based predictions with structural predictions from AlphaFold2 (or AlphaFold3). When the user provides an AF2 predicted structure (PDB/CIF file) and its associated PAE (predicted aligned error) JSON file, Disobind:

1. **Extracts confident AF2 interactions** — residue pairs where the inter-protein distance is < 8Å, the per-residue pLDDT > 70, and the PAE < 5.
2. **Merges predictions** — takes the element-wise maximum of the Disobind probability map and the binarized AF2 contact map, combining complementary strengths.

This is particularly valuable because AF2 excels at predicting folded interactions but often fails on disordered regions (low pLDDT), while Disobind is specifically trained on IDR-containing complexes. The fusion leverages each method's strengths.

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L750-L783), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L966-L988)

## Project Structure

```
disobind/
├── run_disobind.py          ← Main entry point (prediction CLI)
├── install.sh               ← Conda environment setup
├── requirements.txt         ← Python dependencies
├── params/                  ← YAML configs for each model version
├── models/                  ← Pre-trained model weights (.pth files)
│   └── Epsilon_3/           ← Organized by Version_6, Version_16, etc.
├── src/                     ← Core source: model architecture, training, losses
│   ├── models/              ← Epsilon_3 definition, layer factories
│   ├── build_model.py       ← Model construction utilities
│   ├── loss.py              ← Loss functions (SE loss, BCE, count-regularized)
│   ├── metrics.py           ← Evaluation metrics
│   └── model_versions.py    ← Config generation for training
├── dataset/                 ← Dataset construction pipeline (4 steps)
│   ├── 1_disobind_databases.py  ← Step 1: collect PDB IDs from disorder DBs
│   ├── 2_create_database_dataset_files.py  ← Step 2: download PDBs, create binary complexes
│   ├── 3_create_merged_binary_complexes.py ← Step 3: merge overlapping complexes
│   ├── 4_create_non_redundant_dataset.py   ← Step 4: non-redundant train/test split
│   └── create_input_embeddings.py          ← ProtT5 embedding generation
├── database/                ← Input files and raw database dumps
│   ├── input_files/         ← Pre-processed CSV/TSV files
│   └── raw/                 ← Raw downloads from DIBS, MFIB, DisProt, etc.
├── analysis/                ← Analysis scripts, benchmarking, figure generation
└── example/                 ← Example input files (test.csv, test.fasta)
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L10), [dataset/README.md](/dataset/README.md#L1-L27), [src/README.md](/src/README.md#L1-L11)

## Key Technical Dependencies

| Category | Package | Purpose |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Deep Learning | PyTorch 2.0.1 | Model inference and training |
| Protein Embeddings | Transformers 4.33.1, ProtT5 (via HuggingFace) | 1024-dim per-residue embeddings |
| Structure Parsing | Biopython 1.81 | PDB/CIF file parsing for AF2 integration |
| Configuration | OmegaConf 2.2.2 | YAML-based model config management |
| Data | h5py 3.7.0, pandas 1.5.0, numpy 1.24.3 | Embedding storage (HDF5), tabular I/O |
| Calibration | betacal 1.1.0 | Beta calibration for probability outputs |

Sources: [requirements.txt](/requirements.txt#L1-L34), [install.sh](/install.sh#L1-L27)

## Intended Audience and Constraints

Disobind is designed for researchers studying **intrinsically disordered protein interactions**. There are three important constraints to keep in mind:

- **Binary complexes only** — Disobind processes pairs of proteins (AB). For higher-order complexes (ABC), run each pair independently (AB, AC, BC).
- **Protein 1 must be an IDR** — the first protein in the pair is assumed to be disordered; Protein 2 may or may not be disordered.
- **Interacting pairs only** — Disobind predicts *where* two proteins interact, not *whether* they interact. The input pair should be known or suspected to bind.

> [!TIP]
> Disobind is both testable and parallelizable. Multi-core parallelism is used for UniProt sequence downloads, and GPU inference is supported via the `-d cuda` flag. A Google Colab notebook is also available for zero-install usage.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L40-L48), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L44-L84)

# Quick Start



Get Disobind running in under five minutes — from cloning the repository to generating your first intrinsically disordered region (IDR) binding prediction. This page walks you through installation, your first prediction using the bundled example, and the command-line interface you will use every day.

## Prerequisites

Before installing Disobind, ensure your system meets these requirements:

| Requirement | Specification |
|:---|:---|
| **Python** | 3.9 (enforced by conda environment) |
| **Conda** | Miniconda or Anaconda installed |
| **CUDA** *(optional)* | CUDA Toolkit 11.8 + NVIDIA drivers for GPU acceleration |
| **Git** | For cloning the repository |
| **Internet** | Required at first run to download UniProt sequences and ProtT5 embeddings |

> [!TIP]
> Disobind fetches protein sequences from the UniProt API at runtime. Ensure outbound network access is available when running predictions with UniProt IDs for the first time — results are cached locally for subsequent runs.

Sources: [install.sh](/install.sh#L14-L26), [requirements.txt](/requirements.txt#L1-L33)

## Installation

The installation process creates an isolated conda environment named `diso`, installs all Python dependencies, and configures the `PYTHONPATH` so that internal module imports resolve correctly.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["git clone https://github.com/isblab/disobind.git"] --> B["cd disobind/"]
    B --> C["chmod +x install.sh"]
    C --> D["./install.sh"]
    D --> E["conda activate diso"]
    E --> F((Ready to predict))
    
    style A fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32
    style F fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0
```

Execute the following commands in your terminal:

```bash
# 1. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/isblab/disobind.git

# 2. Enter the project directory
cd disobind/

# 3. Make the install script executable and run it
chmod +x install.sh
./install.sh

# 4. Activate the conda environment (do this every session)
conda activate diso
```

The install script performs three actions under the hood: it extracts the ProtTrans archive, appends the project root to `PYTHONPATH` in your `~/.bash_profile`, and creates the `diso` conda environment with all dependencies from `requirements.txt`. Key dependencies include **PyTorch 2.0.1**, **HuggingFace Transformers 4.33.1** (for ProtT5 embeddings), **BioPython 1.81** (for structure parsing), and **OmegaConf 2.2.2** (for YAML model configuration).

Sources: [install.sh](/install.sh#L1-L27), [requirements.txt](/requirements.txt#L1-L33)

## Your First Prediction

Disobind ships with a ready-to-use example in the `example/` directory. The file `example/test.csv` contains two rows: one for a **Disobind-only** prediction and one for a **Disobind+AF2** prediction, both using the prion protein (UniProt ID `P04273`, residues 95–193).

### Run the example

```bash
python run_disobind.py -i csv -f ./example/test.csv
```

This single command triggers the full prediction pipeline: it reads the CSV input, downloads UniProt sequences, generates ProtT5 embeddings, loads the pre-trained Epsilon_3 models, and writes predictions to the `./output/` directory.

### What just happened?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Input CSV"] --> B["Download<br/>UniProt Sequences"]
    B --> C["Generate<br/>ProtT5 Embeddings"]
    C --> D["Load Pre-trained<br/>Epsilon_3 Models"]
    D --> E["Predict Interface<br/>& Contact Maps"]
    E --> F["Write Output<br/>CSV + .npy"]

    style A fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100
    style F fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32
```

After the run completes, inspect the output directory:

```bash
ls ./output/
```

You will find:

| File | Description |
|:---|:---|
| `diso_<entry_id>_interface_cg1.csv` | Disobind interface residue predictions at coarse-grained resolution 1 |
| `af2_<entry_id>_interface_cg1.csv` | AlphaFold2 interface predictions *(Disobind+AF2 rows only)* |
| `diso_af2_<entry_id>_interface_cg1.csv` | Combined Disobind+AF2 predictions *(Disobind+AF2 rows only)* |
| `Predictions.npy` | Full nested dictionary of all predictions (load with `np.load(..., allow_pickle=True)`) |
| `UniProt_seq.json` | Cached UniProt sequences for reuse |
| `p1_p2_test.fasta` | Intermediate FASTA file for embedding generation |

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L111-L126), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L785-L796), [example/test.csv](/example/test.csv#L1-L2)

## Command-Line Interface

All predictions are invoked through `run_disobind.py`. The table below summarizes every available flag:

| Flag | Short | Default | Description |
|:-----|:------|:--------|:------------|
| `--input_type` | `-i` | *(required)* | Input file format: **`csv`** or **`fasta`** |
| `--input` | `-f` | *(required)* | Path to the input file |
| `--max_cores` | `-c` | `2` | Number of CPU cores for parallel UniProt sequence downloads |
| `--output_dir` | `-o` | `output` | Name of the output directory |
| `--device` | `-d` | `cpu` | Compute device: **`cpu`** or **`cuda`** |
| `--cmaps` | `-cm` | `False` | If set, also predict inter-protein **contact maps** (in addition to interface residues) |
| `--coarse` | `-cg` | `1` | Coarse-grained resolution: **`1`**, **`5`**, **`10`**, or **`0`** for all three |

### Common usage patterns

```bash
# Disobind-only: interface residues at CG-1 (fastest, default)
python run_disobind.py -i csv -f ./example/test.csv

# Predict both contact maps AND interface residues
python run_disobind.py -i csv -f ./example/test.csv -cm

# Run at all coarse-grained resolutions (1, 5, 10)
python run_disobind.py -i csv -f ./example/test.csv -cg 0

# Use GPU acceleration
python run_disobind.py -i csv -f ./example/test.csv -d cuda

# Custom output directory and 4 cores for parallel downloads
python run_disobind.py -i csv -f ./example/test.csv -o my_results -c 4

# Use FASTA input instead of CSV
python run_disobind.py -i fasta -f ./example/test.fasta
```

> [!TIP]
> When using `-cg 5` or `-cg 10`, C-terminal residues are discarded if the protein length is not an exact multiple of the kernel size. Use `-cg 1` for residue-level precision, or `-cg 0` to compare predictions across all resolutions.

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L1312-L1357), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L130-L165)

## Preparing Your Input

Disobind accepts two input formats. **CSV** is preferred for batch predictions on proteins with UniProt accessions; **FASTA** supports custom sequences without UniProt entries.

### CSV format — batch predictions

Each row represents one protein pair. Two variants exist depending on whether you want Disobind-only or Disobind+AF2 predictions:

| Mode | Column layout |
|:-----|:-------------|
| **Disobind only** | `UniProt_ID1, start1, end1, UniProt_ID2, start2, end2` |
| **Disobind+AF2** | `UniProt_ID1, start1, end1, UniProt_ID2, start2, end2, AF2_struct_path, AF2_pae_path, chain1, chain2, offset1, offset2` |

The bundled example illustrates both modes in a single file:

```csv
P04273,95,193,P04273,95,192
P04273,95,193,P04273,95,193,./example/unrelaxed_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.pdb,./example/pae_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.json,B,C,0,0
```

**Key constraints to remember:**

- **Protein 1 must be an IDR** (intrinsically disordered region); Protein 2 may or may not be disordered.
- The input pair is **assumed to be interacting** — Disobind predicts *where* they interact, not *whether* they interact.
- For **non-binary complexes** (e.g., ABC), decompose into binary pairs (AB, BC, AC) and run each separately.
- The `offset` values account for residue position differences between the AF2 structure and UniProt numbering. Set to `0` if the AF2 structure covers the full UniProt sequence or exactly the specified fragment.

### FASTA format — custom sequences

For proteins without a UniProt accession, provide sequences directly:

```
>ID1, start1, end1, AF2_struct_path, AF2_pae_path, chain1, offset1
PROTEIN1SEQUENCE...
>ID2, start2, end2, AF2_struct_path, AF2_pae_path, chain2, offset2
PROTEIN2SEQUENCE...
```

A FASTA file must contain **exactly two entries** (one pair per file). For Disobind-only predictions, omit the AF2 fields: `>ID, start, end`.

Sources: [example/test.csv](/example/test.csv#L1-L2), [example/test.fasta](/example/test.fasta#L1-L5), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L312-L359), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L240-L308)

## Understanding the Output

For each input pair, Disobind produces CSV files with four columns:

| Column | Meaning |
|:-------|:--------|
| **Protein1** | Identifier for protein 1 (the IDR) |
| **Residue1** | Residue position(s) in protein 1 predicted to be involved in binding |
| **Protein2** | Identifier for protein 2 (the binding partner) |
| **Residue2** | Residue position(s) in protein 2 predicted to be involved in binding |

**Interpretation differs by prediction type:**

- **Contact map** (`-cm` flag): Each row specifies a specific pairwise interaction — e.g., residue 10 in Protein1 interacts with residue 40 in Protein2.
- **Interface residues** (default): Rows list residues on each side that participate in the interface — e.g., residues 10, 14, 125 in Protein1 interact with *one or more* of residues 40, 44, 80 in Protein2.

When Disobind+AF2 is used, three CSV variants are generated: `diso_` (Disobind alone), `af2_` (AlphaFold2 confident contacts), and `diso_af2_` (element-wise maximum of both methods).

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L893-L960), [README.md](/README.md#L103-L113)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Problem | Cause | Solution |
|:--------|:------|:---------|
| `ModuleNotFoundError` for `src` or `dataset` | `PYTHONPATH` not set | Run `source ~/.bash_profile` or manually `export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/disobind:$PYTHONPATH` |
| `Unable to download seq for Uniprot ID` | Network issue or invalid UniProt ID | Verify the UniProt ID at [uniprot.org](https://www.uniprot.org); check internet connectivity |
| `Incorrect input format` | Wrong number of CSV columns | Use exactly 6 columns (Disobind-only) or 12 columns (Disobind+AF2) |
| `Incorrect coarse-grained resolution` | Invalid `-cg` value | Choose from `0`, `1`, `5`, or `10` |
| CUDA out of memory | Large protein on GPU | Switch to `-d cpu` or reduce batch size |
| `Output directory already exists` | Re-running into same output folder | Answer `n` to continue, or specify a new `-o` directory name |

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L94-L98), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L224-L236), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L144-L146), [install.sh](/install.sh#L7-L11)

# Input Formats and Examples



Disobind accepts protein pair inputs in two formats—**CSV** and **FASTA**—each designed for a different use case. The CSV format is the preferred and more flexible option, supporting batch prediction of multiple protein pairs by referencing UniProt accessions. The FASTA format enables prediction for custom sequences that lack a UniProt entry, but is limited to a single pair per file. Both formats also support the optional **Disobind+AF2** mode, where you supply AlphaFold2 structural predictions alongside the sequence information for refined results.

## Input Requirements

Before preparing your input files, keep these constraints in mind:

| Requirement | Detail |
|:---|:---|
| **Binary complexes only** | Disobind operates on pairs (AB). For non-binary complexes (ABC), decompose into binary pairs (AB, BC, AC) and run each separately. |
| **Protein 1 must be an IDR** | The first protein in the pair is assumed to be an intrinsically disordered region. Protein 2 may or may not be disordered. |
| **Interacting pair assumed** | Disobind predicts *where* the proteins interact (contact maps and interface residues), not *whether* they interact. |
| **Residue range validation** | The specified `start`–`end` range must not exceed the length of the corresponding protein sequence. |

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L4-L14), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L435-L453), [README.md](/README.md#L43-L46)

## CSV Format (Preferred)

The CSV format is the recommended way to provide input. Each row represents one protein fragment pair for which Disobind predictions are required. There are **two variants** depending on whether you want Disobind-only or Disobind+AF2 predictions.

### Disobind-Only (6 fields)

```
UniProt_ID1,start1,end1,UniProt_ID2,start2,end2
```

| Field | Description | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `UniProt_ID1` | UniProt accession for the IDR (Protein 1) | `P04273` |
| `start1` | Start residue position of Protein 1 fragment (UniProt numbering) | `95` |
| `end1` | End residue position of Protein 1 fragment (UniProt numbering) | `193` |
| `UniProt_ID2` | UniProt accession for the binding partner (Protein 2) | `P04273` |
| `start2` | Start residue position of Protein 2 fragment | `95` |
| `end2` | End residue position of Protein 2 fragment | `192` |

When using this format, Disobind automatically downloads the full UniProt sequences for both accessions via the UniProt REST API, then extracts the specified residue fragments for prediction.

### Disobind+AF2 (12 fields)

```
UniProt_ID1,start1,end1,UniProt_ID2,start2,end2,AF2_struct_file,AF2_pae_file,chain1,chain2,offset1,offset2
```

| Field | Description | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `AF2_struct_file` | Path to the AF2 predicted structure file (`.pdb` or `.cif`) | `./example/unrelaxed_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.pdb` |
| `AF2_pae_file` | Path to the AF2 PAE data file (`.json`) | `./example/pae_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.json` |
| `chain1` | Chain ID in the AF2 structure corresponding to Protein 1 | `B` |
| `chain2` | Chain ID in the AF2 structure corresponding to Protein 2 | `C` |
| `offset1` | Residue position offset for Protein 1 (0 if AF2 structure matches UniProt range) | `0` |
| `offset2` | Residue position offset for Protein 2 (0 if AF2 structure matches UniProt range) | `0` |

> [!TIP]
> The **offset** fields account for differences between AF2 residue numbering and UniProt numbering. Set both to `0` if the AF2 structure corresponds to the full UniProt sequence or exactly to the specified fragment range.

### CSV Example

The repository includes a ready-to-run example at `example/test.csv`:

```csv
P04273,95,193,P04273,95,192
P04273,95,193,P04273,95,193,./example/unrelaxed_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.pdb,./example/pae_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.json,B,C,0,0
```

- **Row 1**: A Disobind-only prediction for the prion protein (P04273) fragment 95–193 interacting with itself at fragment 95–192.
- **Row 2**: A Disobind+AF2 prediction for the same prion protein fragment 95–193, augmented with an AF2 multimer model (chains B and C, no residue offset).

Sources: [example/test.csv](/example/test.csv#L1-L2), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L312-L359), [README.md](/README.md#L52-L65)

## FASTA Format

The FASTA format is for proteins **without a UniProt accession**. You provide the amino acid sequences directly. Each file must contain **exactly two entries**—one for each protein in the pair.

### Disobind-Only (3 header fields)

```
>Protein_ID1,start1,end1
SEQUENCE1
>Protein_ID2,start2,end2
SEQUENCE2
```

### Disobind+AF2 (7 header fields)

```
>Protein_ID1,start1,end1,AF2_struct_file,AF2_pae_file,chain1,offset1
SEQUENCE1
>Protein_ID2,start2,end2,AF2_struct_file,AF2_pae_file,chain2,offset2
SEQUENCE2
```

| Header Field | Disobind-Only | Disobind+AF2 | Description |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---|
| `Protein_ID` | ✓ | ✓ | An identifier for the protein (used in output labeling) |
| `start` | ✓ | ✓ | Start residue position of the fragment |
| `end` | ✓ | ✓ | End residue position of the fragment |
| `AF2_struct_file` | — | ✓ | Path to the AF2 structure file (`.pdb`/`.cif`) |
| `AF2_pae_file` | — | ✓ | Path to the AF2 PAE file (`.json`) |
| `chain` | — | ✓ | Chain ID in the AF2 structure for this protein |
| `offset` | — | ✓ | Residue position offset for this protein |

> [!TIP]
> In FASTA mode, the provided sequence is assumed to be the **full protein sequence**. Disobind uses this sequence directly instead of fetching from UniProt. The `start`/`end` values define the fragment to extract from this full sequence for prediction.

### FASTA Example

The repository includes an example at `example/test.fasta`:

```
>prion,95,193,./example/unrelaxed_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.pdb,./example/pae_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.json,B,0
MANLSYWLLALFVAMWTDVGLCKKRPKPGGWNTGGSRYPGQGSPGGNRYPPQGGGTWGQPHGGGWGQPHGGGWGQPHGGGWGQPHGGGWGQGGGTHNQWNKPSKPKTNMKHMAGAAAAGAVVGGLGGYMLGSAMSRPMMHFGNDWEDRYYRENMNRYPNQVYYRPVDQYNNQNNFVHDCVNITIKQHTVTTTTKGENFTETDIKIMERVVEQMCTTQYQKESQAYYDGRRSSAVLFSSPPVILLISFLIFLMVG

>prion,95,193,./example/unrelaxed_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.pdb,./example/pae_model_4_multimer_v3_pred_4.json,C,0
MANLSYWLLALFVAMWTDVGLCKKRPKPGGWNTGGSRYPGQGSPGGNRYPPQGGGTWGQPHGGGWGQPHGGGWGQPHGGGWGQPHGGGWGQGGGTHNQWNKPSKPKTNMKHMAGAAAAGAVVGGLGGYMLGSAMSRPMMHFGNDWEDRYYRENMNRYPNQVYYRPVDQYNNQNNFVHDCVNITIKQHTVTTTTKGENFTETDIKIMERVVEQMCTTQYQKESQAYYDGRRSSAVLFSSPPVILLISFLIFLMVG
```

This defines a Disobind+AF2 prediction for the prion protein homodimer, where both chains map to the same AF2 multimer structure (chains B and C respectively).

Sources: [example/test.fasta](/example/test.fasta#L1-L5), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L240-L308), [README.md](/README.md#L67-L72)

## AF2 Supplementary Files

When using Disobind+AF2 mode, you must provide two additional files from your AlphaFold2 multimer prediction:

| File | Format | Content | Key Field |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Structure file** | `.pdb` or `.cif` | 3D coordinates with per-residue pLDDT scores in the B-factor column | Atom coordinates, B-factor (pLDDT) |
| **PAE file** | `.json` | Predicted Aligned Error matrix | `predicted_aligned_error` |

The PAE JSON file must be a JSON array containing an object with the key `"predicted_aligned_error"`, which stores the asymmetric PAE matrix as a 2D array. Disobind symmetrizes this internally by computing `(PAE + PAE^T) / 2`. The structure file is parsed using Biopython's `PDBParser` (for `.pdb`) or `MMCIFParser` (for `.cif`), and per-residue pLDDT scores are read from the Cα B-factor column.

### Confidence Filtering

Disobind applies three internal confidence thresholds when combining AF2 predictions:

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| `dist_threshold` | 8 Å | Maximum Cα–Cα distance to define a residue contact |
| `plddt_threshold` | 70 | Minimum pLDDT score to consider a residue confidently predicted |
| `pae_threshold` | 5 | Maximum PAE value to consider a residue pair confidently aligned |

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L966-L1090), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L70-L76)

## Choosing Between CSV and FASTA

| Feature | CSV | FASTA |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| Multiple pairs per file | ✓ | ✗ |
| UniProt accession required | ✓ | ✗ |
| Custom sequences supported | ✗ | ✓ |
| Disobind-only mode | ✓ | ✓ |
| Disobind+AF2 mode | ✓ | ✓ |
| Auto sequence download | ✓ | ✗ |

Use **CSV** when your proteins have UniProt entries—you can batch dozens of pairs in a single file and let Disobind fetch the sequences automatically. Use **FASTA** when working with custom or synthetic sequences that are not deposited in UniProt.

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L212-L237), [README.md](/README.md#L48-L51)

## Running the Example

Execute Disobind with the provided example input using:

```bash
python run_disobind.py -i csv -f ./example/test.csv
```

For the FASTA example:

```bash
python run_disobind.py -i fasta -f ./example/test.fasta
```

Both commands use default settings: interface residue prediction at coarse-grained resolution 1 on CPU. See [Quick Start](2-quick-start) for the full list of command-line flags and [Output Interpretation](10-output-interpretation) for understanding the results.

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L1312-L1357), [README.md](/README.md#L76-L80)

## Format Validation

Disobind performs strict validation on your input. The following errors will be raised if the format is incorrect:

| Condition | Error Type | Message |
|:---|:---|:---|
| CSV row has neither 6 nor 12 comma-separated fields | `ValueError` | `Incorrect input format...` |
| FASTA file contains ≠ 2 entries | `ValueError` | `Expected exactly 2 FASTA entries, found N...` |
| FASTA header has neither 3 nor 7 comma-separated fields | `ValueError` | `Incorrect input header format...` |
| Specified residue range exceeds sequence length | `ValueError` | `Sequence length (L residues) is shorter than the specified residue range S-E...` |
| AF2 structure file is not `.pdb` or `.cif` | `ValueError` | `Incorrect file format.. Supported .pdb/.cif only.` |
| PAE file is not `.json` | `ValueError` | `Incorrect file format.. Supported .json only.` |
| PAE JSON missing `predicted_aligned_error` key | `ValueError` | `PAE matrix not found...` |


# Architecture Overview



Disobind is a **dual-purpose deep learning system** that predicts residue-level interactions between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and their structured partner proteins, and optionally fuses its predictions with AlphaFold2 structural confidence signals. The architecture spans four conceptual layers — a user-facing prediction orchestrator, a neural network engine built on the Epsilon_3 model family, a protein language model embedding pipeline, and a multi-stage dataset construction framework — each with well-defined responsibilities and data contracts. This page maps the complete system topology, traces the primary data flows, and identifies the key abstraction boundaries that govern how these layers interact.

## System Topology

The following diagram presents the complete Disobind architecture at a glance, from user input through embedding generation, model inference, and optional AF2 fusion, down to the dataset construction and training subsystems that produce the deployed models.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph UserLayer["User Interface Layer"]
        INPUT["Input File<br/>(CSV / FASTA)"]
        CLI["run_disobind.py<br/>Disobind class"]
    end

    subgraph EmbeddingLayer["Embedding Layer"]
        UNIPROT["UniProt API<br/>Sequence Download"]
        FASTA_GEN["FASTA Generation"]
        PROTT5["ProtT5 Encoder<br/>"1024-dim residues""]
        H5["H5 Embedding Store"]
    end

    subgraph ModelLayer["Model Engine Layer"]
        CONFIG["YAML Config= params/"]
        FACTORY["get_model()<br/>Model Factory"]
        EPS3["Epsilon_3 Model<br/>src/models/E:3.py"]
        REGISTRY["Model Registry<br/>analysis/params.py"]
    end

    subgraph PredictionLayer["Prediction & Fusion Layer"]
        DISO_PRED["Disobind Predictions"]
        AF2["AfPrediction<br/>AlphaFold2 Parser"]
        FUSION["Disobind+AF2 Fusion<br/>"element-wise max""]
        OUTPUT["Output CSVs + NPZ"]
    end

    subgraph TrainingLayer["Training Subsystem"]
        TRAINER["Trainer<br/>src/build_model.py"]
        LOSS["Loss Functions<br/>src/loss.py"]
        METRICS["Metrics<br/>src/metrics.py"]
        DLOADER["DatasetLoader<br/>src/dataset_loaders.py"]
    end

    subgraph DataLayer["Dataset Construction Pipeline"]
        S1["Step 1: Parse DBs<br/>1_disobind_databases.py"]
        S2["Step 2: PDB → Dataset<br/>2_create_database_dataset_files.py"]
        S3["Step 3: Merge Complexes<br/>3_create_merged_binary_complexes.py"]
        S4["Step 4: Non-Redundant Split<br/>4_create_non_redundant_dataset.py"]
    end

    INPUT --> CLI
    CLI --> UNIPROT
    UNIPROT --> FASTA_GEN
    FASTA_GEN --> PROTT5
    PROTT5 --> H5
    H5 --> CLI

    CLI --> REGISTRY
    REGISTRY --> CONFIG
    CONFIG --> FACTORY
    FACTORY --> EPS3
    H5 --> EPS3
    EPS3 --> DISO_PRED

    CLI --> AF2
    AF2 --> FUSION
    DISO_PRED --> FUSION
    FUSION --> OUTPUT
    DISO_PRED --> OUTPUT

    TRAINER --> LOSS
    TRAINER --> METRICS
    TRAINER --> DLOADER
    DLOADER --> TRAINER

    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4
    S4 --> DLOADER
```

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L1-L60), [src/models/get_model.py](/src/models/get_model.py#L1-L27), [analysis/params.py](/analysis/params.py#L1-L60)

## Prediction Orchestrator — The `Disobind` Class

The `Disobind` class in `run_disobind.py` is the **single entry point** for all inference workflows. It accepts either CSV or FASTA input specifying one or more IDR–partner protein pairs, and coordinates the full prediction lifecycle: downloading UniProt sequences, generating ProtT5 embeddings, loading the appropriate model variants, running inference across all requested tasks and coarse-graining levels, optionally parsing AlphaFold2 structures, and fusing predictions.

The orchestrator maintains a `self.objective` list of four parameters — `[task_type, bin_size, bin_input, single_output]` — that is dynamically reconfigured per model variant via `apply_settings()`. This allows the same Epsilon_3 architecture to switch between **interaction** (contact map) and **interface** (residue classification) prediction tasks, and between fine-grained (CG=1) and coarse-grained (CG=5, 10) resolutions without any architectural changes.

| Orchestrator Attribute | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `embedding_type` | Protein language model for embeddings | `"T5"` (ProtT5) |
| `scope` | Global vs. local embedding context | `"global"` |
| `threshold` | Contact probability binarization cutoff | `0.5` |
| `dist_threshold` | Distance cutoff for AF2 contact definition (Å) | `8` |
| `plddt_threshold` | pLDDT confidence cutoff for AF2 | `70` |
| `pae_threshold` | PAE confidence cutoff for AF2 | `5` |
| `batch_size` | Pairs per embedding batch | `200` |
| `parameters` | Model version → parameter file mapping | `parameter_files(19)` |

> [!TIP]
> The `parameters` dict from `analysis/params.py` is the **central model registry** — it maps each `(objective, CG)` combination to a specific model version and checkpoint filename. Changing the `model_version` argument to `parameter_files()` switches between entirely different model families.

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L46-L107), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L155-L198)

## Dual Prediction Tasks

Disobind simultaneously addresses two complementary prediction objectives, each available at three coarse-graining resolutions:

| Task | Output Shape | Semantic Meaning | Model Family |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Interaction** | `[L1, L2]` | Per-residue-pair contact probability | Epsilon_3 v6.x |
| **Interface** | `[L1+L2, 1]` | Per-residue interface membership probability | Epsilon_3 v16.x |

**Coarse-graining (CG)** pools contiguous residues into "beads" of size *k*, reducing the output dimensionality by a factor of *k* along each protein axis. CG=1 is residue-level; CG=5 groups 5 residues per bead; CG=10 groups 10. This is achieved via `MaxPool2d` on the target during training and on the output during inference, with no modification to the input embeddings. The trade-off is spatial resolution versus prediction confidence on longer sequences.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph CG1["CG = 1"]
        R1["r₁ r₂ r₃ r₄ r₅ r₆ r₇ r₈ r₉ r₁₀"]
    end
    subgraph CG5["CG = 5"]
        B1["[r₁-r₅]"] 
        B2["[r₆-r₁₀]"]
    end
    subgraph CG10["CG = 10"]
        B3["[r₁-r₁₀]"]
    end
    CG1 -->|"MaxPool2d<br/>k=5"| CG5
    CG5 -->|"MaxPool2d<br/>k=2"| CG10
```

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L108-L154), [src/utils.py](/src/utils.py#L72-L170), [analysis/params.py](/analysis/params.py#L27-L60)

## Epsilon_3 Model Architecture

The **Epsilon_3** model is the sole neural network architecture currently deployed in Disobind. It implements a **projection–interaction–processing–output** pipeline that transforms two protein embedding sequences into pairwise interaction predictions. The forward pass proceeds through four distinct blocks:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    E1["e₁ ∈ ℝ^(L1×1024)"] --> PROJ["Projection Block"]
    E2["e₂ ∈ ℝ^(L2×1024)"] --> PROJ
    PROJ -->|"z₁ ∈ ℝ^(L1×d), z₂ ∈ ℝ^(L2×d)"| TENSOR["Interaction Tensor<br/>z₁ ⊙ z₂ᵀ ∈ ℝ^(L1×L2×d)"]
    TENSOR --> IFACE{"Task?"}
    IFACE -->|"interaction"| FLAT["Flatten → ℝ^(L1·L2×d)"]
    IFACE -->|"interface"| AVG2D["avg2d → ℝ^((L1+L2)×d)"]
    FLAT --> HIDDEN["Hidden Block<br/>(vanilla / residual)"]
    AVG2D --> HIDDEN
    HIDDEN --> OUT["Output Block<br/>Linear → Sigmoid"]
    OUT --> PRED["Predictions ∈ (0,1)"]
```

### Projection Block

Each protein's 1024-dimensional ProtT5 embeddings are projected to a lower-dimensional space (*d* = 128 or 256) via a configurable layer sequence. The `projection_layer` config parameter `[dim, type, bias, multiplier, sharing]` controls five properties:

- **dim**: Projection dimensionality (128 or 256)
- **type**: Normalization placement — `vanilla` (Linear→Activation), `ln1` (LayerNorm→Linear→Activation), `ln2` (Linear→Activation→LayerNorm), plus `in1/in2/bn1/bn2` variants
- **sharing**: `"separate"` creates two independent projection layers (one per protein); `""` shares a single layer

### Interaction Tensor

The projected embeddings *z₁* and *z₂* are combined via an outer-product-style operation to form an interaction tensor of shape `[N, L1, L2, d]`. For the **interaction** task, this tensor is simply flattened to `[N, L1×L2, d]`. For the **interface** task, a masked `avg2d` operation reduces along each axis to produce per-protein interface feature vectors concatenated to `[N, L1+L2, d]`.

### Hidden and Output Blocks

The hidden block supports two modes: **vanilla** (direct pass-through with downsampling→upsampling layers) and **residual** (with a skip connection and optional AddNorm). The output block applies a final `Linear(d, 1)` projection followed by sigmoid activation. An optional **temperature scaling** parameter can be learned or fixed for calibration.

Sources: [src/models/Epsilon_3.py](/src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L28-L145), [src/models/get_layers.py](/src/models/get_layers.py#L1-L100), [src/models/get_activation.py](/src/models/get_activation.py#L1-L78)

## Model Factory and Configuration Pipeline

Model instantiation follows a strict **configuration-driven factory pattern**. YAML files in `params/` define the complete model architecture, dataset paths, and training hyperparameters. The `get_model()` factory in `src/models/get_model.py` reads the `Model` field from the config and dispatches to the appropriate constructor.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    YAML["YAML Config<br/>params/Model_config_*.yml"] -->|"OmegaConf.load()"| OMEGA["OmegaConf Dict"]
    OMEGA -->|".conf.model_params"| FACTORY["get_model(config)"]
    FACTORY -->|"config.Model == 'Epsilon_3'"| EPS3["Epsilon_3(**config)"]
    OMEGA -->|".conf.train_params"| TRAINER["Trainer(config, device)"]
    OMEGA -->|".conf.dataset"| DSET["DatasetLoader(config, seed)"]
```

The `model_versions.py` script is the **config generator** — it programmatically constructs the full YAML config from Python dictionaries, supporting ablation sweeps over projection dimensions, layer counts, dropout rates, and activation functions. This separation ensures that every deployed model checkpoint has a corresponding reproducible configuration file.

| Config Section | Key Parameters | Controls |
|---|---|---|
| `model_params` | `emb_size`, `projection_layer`, `num_hid_layers`, `dropouts`, `activation1/2`, `objective` | Epsilon_3 architecture |
| `dataset` | `input_files`, `train/dev/test_file`, `batch_size`, `batch_shuffle` | Data loading |
| `train_params` | `loss`, `optimizer`, `learning_rate`, `scheduler`, `max_epochs`, `contact_threshold` | Training loop |

Sources: [src/models/get_model.py](/src/models/get_model.py#L1-L27), [src/model_versions.py](/src/model_versions.py#L1-L154), [params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.1.yml](/params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.1.yml#L1-L121)

## Embedding Generation Pipeline

Disobind uses **protein language model embeddings** as its sole input representation — no evolutionary information (MSA) or structural features are required at inference time. The `Embeddings` class in `dataset/create_input_embeddings.py` orchestrates the pipeline:

1. **Sequence Retrieval**: UniProt IDs are resolved to amino acid sequences via the UniProt API (with multiprocess parallelism)
2. **FASTA Generation**: Sequences are written to a FASTA file, either full-length (global scope) or fragment-only (local scope)
3. **Encoder Inference**: The FASTA file is fed to a protein language model encoder, producing per-residue embeddings stored in HDF5 format

| Encoder | Embedding Dim | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ProtT5** (default) | 1024 | ProtTrans / HuggingFace | Primary |
| ProstT5 | 1024 | ProtTrans (3D-aware) | Supported |
| ESM2-650M | 1280 | Meta ESM | Supported |
| protBERT | 1024 | ProtBERT | Supported |
| ProSE | 6165 | ProSE | Supported |

The default **ProtT5 global embeddings** encode each residue in the context of the full protein sequence, capturing disorder-relevant sequential patterns without requiring any structural input.

Sources: [dataset/create_input_embeddings.py](/dataset/create_input_embeddings.py#L38-L131), [dataset/utility.py](/dataset/utility.py#L96-L140)

## AlphaFold2 Fusion (Disobind+AF2)

When users provide AlphaFold2 predicted structures and PAE JSON files, Disobind performs a **complementary fusion** strategy. The `AfPrediction` class parses the AF2 structure to extract confident inter-chain contacts (filtering by pLDDT > 70 and PAE < 5), then the orchestrator computes an element-wise maximum between the Disobind probability map and the binarized AF2 contact map:

```
diso_af2[i,j] = max(disobind_pred[i,j], af2_contact[i,j])
```

This fusion is motivated by the complementary strengths: Disobind captures IDR-specific interaction patterns that AF2 often misses (due to low pLDDT in disordered regions), while AF2 provides high-confidence structural contacts when its predictions are reliable. The result is that **Disobind+AF2 recovers contacts that either method alone would miss**.

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L700-L770), [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L1100-L1200)

## Training Subsystem

The `Trainer` class in `src/build_model.py` extends `nn.Module` and encapsulates the full training lifecycle. It supports multiple optimizers (Adam, AdamW, SGD with amsgrad), learning rate schedulers (exponential, cyclic, multistep, linear, SWA), and gradient clipping. The training loop computes loss via a pluggable loss function registry, evaluates with `torchmetrics` binary classification metrics, and optionally applies post-hoc calibration (Platt scaling, beta calibration, isotonic regression).

The loss function library in `src/loss.py` includes **BCE**, **BCEWithLogits** (with class weighting and positional weighting), **Focal Loss**, **Singularity Enhanced Loss** (the default `se_loss`), and composite losses. The Singularity Enhanced Loss is specifically designed for the extreme class imbalance in contact maps by applying an asymmetric penalty that amplifies gradients for the minority (contact) class.

Sources: [src/build_model.py](/src/build_model.py#L24-L90), [src/loss.py](/src/loss.py#L1-L60), [src/metrics.py](/src/metrics.py#L1-L62)

## Dataset Construction Pipeline

The training data flows through a **four-step pipeline** in the `dataset/` directory, transforming raw database entries into non-redundant, pre-split numpy arrays ready for embedding:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    RAW["Raw Database Files<br/>DIBS, MFIB, FuzDB,<br/>PDBtot, PDBcdr, DisProt,<br/>IDEAL, MobiDB"]
    
    S1["Step 1: Parse Databases<br/>1_disobind_databases.py<br/>→ Merged PDB ID lists"]
    
    S2["Step 2: PDB → Dataset Files<br/>2_create_database_dataset_files.py<br/>→ Download PDBs, map residues,<br/>   identify IDR-containing complexes"]
    
    S3["Step 3: Merge Binary Complexes<br/>3_create_merged_binary_complexes.py<br/>→ Validate, deduplicate,<br/>   merge overlapping fragments"]
    
    S4["Step 4: Non-Redundant Split<br/>4_create_non_redundant_dataset.py<br/>→ Cluster at sequence identity,<br/>   split Train/Dev/Test"]

    RAW --> S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4
    S4 -->|"Train/Dev/Test .npy"| EMB["Embedding Generation<br/>create_input_embeddings.py"]
    EMB -->|".h5 + .npy"| TRAIN["Model Training"]
```

- **Step 1** parses five structure databases (DIBS, MFIB, FuzDB, PDBtot-cdr) and three disorder databases (DisProt, IDEAL, MobiDB) to produce a merged list of PDB IDs containing IDRs in complexes
- **Step 2** downloads PDB structures, maps UniProt→PDB residue positions via SIFTS, and identifies binary IDR–partner complexes
- **Step 3** validates complexes, merges overlapping fragments from different PDB depositions, and creates contact maps from Cα coordinates
- **Step 4** clusters sequences by identity to enforce non-redundancy between train, dev, and test splits

Sources: [dataset/1_disobind_databases.py](/dataset/1_disobind_databases.py#L1-L50), [dataset/2_create_database_dataset_files.py](/dataset/2_create_database_dataset_files.py#L1-L50), [dataset/3_create_merged_binary_complexes.py](/dataset/3_create_merged_binary_complexes.py#L1-L50)

## Project Directory Structure

```
disobind/
├── run_disobind.py            # Prediction orchestrator (Disobind + AfPrediction classes)
├── src/
│   ├── models/
│   │   ├── Epsilon_3.py       # Core neural network architecture
│   │   ├── get_model.py       # Model factory (config → model instance)
│   │   ├── get_layers.py      # Layer constructors (projection, up/downsampling)
│   │   └── get_activation.py  # Activation function registry
│   ├── build_model.py         # Trainer class (training loop, optimizer, scheduler)
│   ├── dataset_loaders.py     # Dataset splitting and DataLoader creation
│   ├── loss.py                # Loss function library (BCE, Focal, SE, etc.)
│   ├── metrics.py             # Evaluation metrics (torchmetrics wrappers)
│   ├── model_versions.py      # Config generator (Python → YAML)
│   └── utils.py               # Input preparation, oversampling, plotting utilities
├── dataset/
│   ├── 1_disobind_databases.py       # Step 1: Parse structure/disorder databases
│   ├── 2_create_database_dataset_files.py  # Step 2: PDB download & IDR identification
│   ├── 3_create_merged_binary_complexes.py # Step 3: Merge & validate complexes
│   ├── 4_create_non_redundant_dataset.py   # Step 4: Non-redundant splitting
│   ├── create_input_embeddings.py    # ProtT5 embedding generation
│   ├── from_APIs_with_love.py        # API clients (UniProt, PDB, SIFTS)
│   ├── utility.py                    # PDB parsing, contact maps, coordinate extraction
│   └── prepare_entry_from_pdb.py     # Single PDB entry processing
├── models/                    # Trained model checkpoints (Epsilon_3/Version_*)
├── params/                    # YAML configuration files for each model version
├── analysis/                  # Evaluation scripts, benchmark analysis, parameter registry
│   └── params.py              # Model version → checkpoint mapping (the registry)
└── database/
    ├── input_files/           # Processed database CSVs, merged PDB lists
    └── raw/                   # Raw database downloads (DIBS, DisProt, IDEAL, etc.)
```

> [!TIP]
> The `models/` and `params/` directories are **paired by convention**: every `models/Epsilon_3/Version_X/Y.pth` checkpoint has a corresponding `params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_X.yml`. The `analysis/params.py` registry is the authoritative mapping from `(task, CG)` → `(model_version, checkpoint_filename)`.

Sources: [run_disobind.py](/run_disobind.py#L1-L60), [src/models/Epsilon_3.py](/src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L28-L80), [dataset/3_create_merged_binary_complexes.py](/dataset/3_create_merged_binary_complexes.py#L55-L100)

## Architectural Design Principles

Three principles govern the Disobind architecture:

**Separation of embedding from inference.** Protein language model embeddings are pre-computed and stored on disk (HDF5), decoupling the expensive encoder forward pass from the lightweight Epsilon_3 inference. This enables batch embedding of thousands of protein pairs followed by fast model evaluation.

**Configuration-driven model diversity.** A single Epsilon_3 architecture class serves all six deployed model variants (2 tasks × 3 CG levels) through YAML configuration alone. No code changes are required to switch between interaction and interface prediction, or between fine-grained and coarse-grained resolutions.

**Complementary fusion over replacement.** The Disobind+AF2 fusion strategy reflects the architectural insight that IDR interactions require specialized models (Disobind) that capture what general structure predictors (AF2) miss, rather than competing with them. The element-wise max fusion is the simplest instantiation of this principle — future extensions could learn adaptive fusion weights.

## Suggested Reading Path

- For the neural network internals: [Epsilon_3 Model Architecture](5-epsilon_3-model-architecture) → [Projection and Interaction Tensor](6-projection-and-interaction-tensor) → [Coarse-Grained Prediction Strategy](7-coarse-grained-prediction-strategy)
- For running predictions: [Embedding Generation with ProtT5](8-embedding-generation-with-prott5) → [Disobind and Disobind+AF2 Prediction](9-disobind-and-disobind-af2-prediction) → [Output Interpretation](10-output-interpretation)
- For training custom models: [Model Training Workflow](11-model-training-workflow) → [Loss Functions and Calibration](12-loss-functions-and-calibration) → [YAML Config Parameters](17-yaml-config-parameters)
- For dataset construction: [Disorder Protein Databases](14-disorder-protein-databases) → [Four-Step Dataset Pipeline](15-four-step-dataset-pipeline) → [Non-Redundant Dataset Splitting](16-non-redundant-dataset-splitting)

# Epsilon_3 Model Architecture



The **Epsilon_3** model is the core neural network of Disobind — a siamese-style architecture that projects per-residue protein embeddings into a shared latent space, constructs a pairwise interaction tensor from the two projected sequences, and then refines that tensor through a bottleneck-hidden block before emitting per-residue or per-pair predictions. Its design is deliberately modular: five sequential blocks — **Projection → Interaction Tensor → Interface → Hidden → Output** — each independently configurable through YAML parameter files, enabling the same `Epsilon_3` class to serve both contact-map prediction (interaction task) and binding-region prediction (interface task) without code changes.

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L1-L21), [get_model.py](src/models/get_model.py#L1-L27)

## High-Level Data Flow

The forward pass orchestrates the five blocks in strict sequence. Given input embeddings **e1** and **e2** (each of shape `[N, L, 1024]` from ProtT5) and an **interaction_mask** marking valid residue pairs, the model produces a prediction tensor **o** whose shape depends on the objective:

```
e1, e2 ──► Projection Block ──► z1, z2 ──► Interaction Tensor ──► Interface Block ──► Hidden Block ──► Output Block ──► o
[N,L,C]     [N,L,D]              [N,L1,L2,2D]    [N, L1+L2, 2D]     [N, L1+L2, state2]   [N, L1+L2, 1]
```

The Mermaid diagram below captures the same flow with the branching paths for each configuration variant:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    E1["e1 [N, L1, 1024]"] --> PROJ["Projection Block"]
    E2["e2 [N, L2, 1024]"] --> PROJ
    MASK["interaction_mask"] --> FWD

    PROJ -->|"z1, z2 [N, L, D]"| IT["Interaction Tensor Block"]
    IT -->|"[N, L1, L2, 2D]"| IB{Interface Block?}

    IB -->|avg1d / avg2d / lin| REDUCED["[N, L1+L2, 2D]"]
    IB -->|interaction obj| FLAT["[N, L1×L2, 2D]"]

    REDUCED --> HB{Hidden Block?}
    FLAT --> HB

    HB -->|vanilla| VAN["Downsample → Upsample"]
    HB -->|residual| RES["(Downsample → Upsample + skip) × N"]
    HB -->|identity| PASS["Pass-through"]

    VAN --> OUT["Output Block"]
    RES --> OUT
    PASS --> OUT

    OUT -->|"+ sigmoid"| PRED["Predictions [0, 1]"]
    OUT -->|"+ temp scaling"| PRED2["Calibrated logits"]

    style PROJ fill:#4a86c8,color:#fff
    style IT fill:#6aa84f,color:#fff
    style IB fill:#e69138,color:#fff
    style HB fill:#cc4125,color:#fff
    style OUT fill:#8e7cc3,color:#fff
```

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L131-L151)

## Projection Block

The projection block maps the high-dimensional ProtT5 embeddings (1024-d) into a compact latent space of dimension `projection_dim` (typically 128 or 256). It is the **only block that touches the raw embeddings**; every subsequent block operates on the projected representations.

### Shared vs. Separate Projections

When `projection_layer[4] == "separate"`, two independent projection networks (`projection_layer1` and `projection_layer2`) are instantiated — one for each protein chain. When set to `""` (empty string, the default across all shipped configs), **both chains share a single projection network**, enforcing a siamese constraint that guarantees the two proteins are mapped into the same latent geometry. This shared-weight design is critical for the outer-product interaction tensor to be geometrically meaningful: the same distance in z-space represents the same degree of interaction potential regardless of which chain a residue belongs to.

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L64-L80), [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L155-L178)

### Projection Layer Variants

The `create_projection_layers` factory in `get_layers.py` supports seven normalization placements, each composing a `Linear → Activation` core with optional pre- or post-normalization:

| Type | Structure | Normalization Placement |
|------|-----------|------------------------|
| `vanilla` | Linear → Activation | None |
| `ln1` | LayerNorm → Linear → Activation | Pre-activation, over input features |
| `ln2` | Linear → Activation → LayerNorm | Post-activation, over output features |
| `in1` | Permute → InstanceNorm1d → Permute → Linear → Activation | Pre-activation, over input features |
| `in2` | Linear → Activation → Permute → InstanceNorm1d → Permute | Post-activation, over output features |
| `bn1` | Permute → BatchNorm1d → Permute → Linear → Activation | Pre-activation, over input features |
| `bn2` | Linear → Activation → Permute → BatchNorm1d → Permute | Post-activation, over output features |

All shipped configurations use **`ln2`** (Linear → ELU → LayerNorm), which stabilizes the projected representations by normalizing after the nonlinearity. The `Permute` helper module swaps `[N, L, C] ↔ [N, C, L]` because PyTorch's `InstanceNorm1d` and `BatchNorm1d` expect the channel dimension first.

Sources: [get_layers.py](src/models/get_layers.py#L8-L84)

### Post-Projection Dropout

After projection, a `Dropout(p=dropouts[0])` is applied independently to both z1 and z2 before they are returned from the `projection_block` method. The default rate is 0.2 across all configurations.

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L175-L178)

## Interaction Tensor Block

The interaction tensor is the mechanism by which Epsilon_3 captures **pairwise residue-residue relationships** between the two projected sequences. It is the architectural centerpiece — the step where the two independently projected chains are combined into a joint representation.

### Aggregation Operations

The `capture_interaction` method implements nine binary operations between projected embeddings z1 and z2. The most important ones for the shipped models are:

| Operation | Formula | Output Shape | Semantic |
|-----------|---------|-------------|----------|
| `op` (outer product) | z1.unsqueeze(2) × z2.unsqueeze(1) | [N, L1, L2, D] | Bilinear interaction strength |
| `od` (outer difference) | \|z1.unsqueeze(2) − z2.unsqueeze(1)\| | [N, L1, L2, D] | Dissimilarity per feature |
| `os` (outer sum) | z1.unsqueeze(2) + z2.unsqueeze(1) | [N, L1, L2, D] | Additive combination |
| `add` | z1 + z2 | [N, L, D] | Element-wise sum (same length) |
| `multiply` | z1 * z2 | [N, L, D] | Hadamard product |
| `dot` | Σ(z1 * z2) | [N, L, 1] | Scalar similarity |
| `cosine` | cos_sim(z1, z2) | [N, L, 1] | Normalized similarity |

### Dual-Operation Strategy

The `input_layer` config specifies a **compound operation** like `"op-od"`, which splits on the hyphen and applies both operations independently, then concatenates the results along the feature dimension. With `op-od`, the final interaction tensor has shape `[N, L1, L2, 2D]` — outer product capturing bilinear coupling and outer difference capturing feature-wise dissimilarity. This dual-channel design gives the downstream layers complementary views: the product highlights when two residues' features align in sign and magnitude, while the absolute difference highlights when they diverge.

### Concatenation Modes

When `input_layer[1] == "vanilla"` (the default), the two operations are computed on the original (z1, z2) pair. When set to `"concat"`, the sequences are first concatenated along the length dimension `[N, L1+L2, D]` and both operations are applied on the self-pair `(z, z)`, producing a square `[N, L1+L2, L1+L2, 2D]` tensor — useful when intra-chain interactions must also be modeled.

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L228-L296)

## Interface Block

The interface block reduces the 4D interaction tensor `[N, L1, L2, C]` to a 2D per-residue representation `[N, L1+L2, C]` suitable for predicting **which residues participate in binding** (as opposed to which specific pairs interact). Three reduction strategies are available:

| Strategy | Mechanism | Detail |
|----------|-----------|--------|
| `avg1d` | Mean along W axis | Simple collapse: `torch.mean(tensor, axis=2)` |
| `avg2d` | Masked bidirectional mean | Computes separate means along L2 and L1 axes with padding-aware masking, then concatenates |
| `lin` | Learned linear projection | Applies a shared `Linear(L, 1)` along each sequence axis, then concatenates |

The **`avg2d`** strategy is the default for interface models (Version 16.x). It is carefully implemented to exclude padding elements from the mean computation: a mask-weighted sum is divided by the count of valid positions (plus ε = 10⁻⁴ for numerical stability), producing two vectors I1 `[N, L1, C]` and I2 `[N, L2, C]` that are concatenated into `[N, L1+L2, C]`. This is the key step that converts a pairwise tensor into a per-chain residue representation.

For **interaction** objectives (Version 6.x), the interface block is bypassed entirely — the 4D tensor is simply reshaped to `[N, L1×L2, C]` for flat per-pair prediction.

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L181-L225)

## Hidden Block

The hidden block processes the feature dimension of the (now 2D) representation through a **downsample-then-upsample bottleneck**. Two architectural variants are supported, controlled by `hidden_block[0]`:

### Vanilla Block

A single pass: **Downsample → Upsample**. No residual connection. Suitable when the bottleneck is shallow (1–3 layers each direction).

### Residual Block

Repeated for `num_blocks` iterations: **(Dropout → Downsample → Upsample + skip)** × N. The skip connection merges the block input with its output using one of three strategies:

| Residual Type | Formula | Notes |
|---------------|---------|-------|
| `None` | o = output (no addition) | Effectively no residual; iterates only the bottleneck |
| `vanilla` | o = output + input | Standard additive skip |
| `addnorm` | o = LayerNorm(output + input) | Normalized residual |
| `addactivnorm` | o = LayerNorm(Activation(output + input)) | Pre-norm activation then normalize |

For InstanceNorm or BatchNorm variants, the tensor is permuted to `[N, C, L]` before normalization and permuted back afterward.

### Downsampling and Upsampling Layers

Each downsampling layer halves the feature dimension: `state → state/scale_factor`, and each upsampling layer doubles it back: `state → state × scale_factor`. Every layer follows the pattern **Norm/Dropout → Linear → Activation**, where the choice between normalization and dropout is exclusive (controlled by `norm[0]`). The feature width progression is tracked and printed at construction time (e.g., `"256 --> 128 --> 64"`).

**Channel state arithmetic** is computed at initialization: `state0 = 2 × projection_dim` (after tensor concatenation), `state1 = state0 / scale^downsample_layers` (bottleneck), `state2 = state1 × scale^upsample_layers` (recovery). The final hidden dimension `state2` determines the input size of the output linear layer.

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L49-L54), [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L300-L335), [get_layers.py](src/models/get_layers.py#L87-L212)

## Output Block

The output block is a simple linear projection followed by optional post-processing:

1. **Linear projection**: `nn.Linear(state2, output_dim)` with configurable bias, mapping the hidden representation to a single logit per residue (or residue pair).
2. **Temperature scaling**: If `temperature` is not `None`, logits are divided by a learnable (or fixed) scalar temperature parameter — a post-hoc calibration technique that softens or sharpens the sigmoid output.
3. **Activation**: If `activation2[1]` is `True`, the final sigmoid is applied, producing probabilities in [0, 1]. Otherwise, raw logits are returned (for use with `BCEWithLogitsLoss` during training).

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L338-L354)

## Activation Function Registry

The `get_activation` factory supports 13 activation functions, enabling extensive experimentation within the same architecture:

| Activation | Trainable Params | Use Case |
|------------|-----------------|----------|
| `relu` | None | Standard baseline |
| `leakyrelu` | None (or fixed slope) | Handles dead neurons |
| `elu` | None | **Default for activation1** — smooth at zero |
| `gelu` | None | Gaussian approximation |
| `celu` | None | Continuously differentiable ELU |
| `prelu` | Yes (per-channel) | Learned negative slope |
| `silu` | None | Swish — self-gated |
| `mish` | None | Smooth non-monotonic |
| `sigmoid` | None | **Default for activation2** — bounded output |
| `tanh` | None | Zero-centered bounded |
| `softmax` | None | Multi-class distribution |
| `logistic_activation` | Yes (η, x₀) | Generalized sigmoid with trainable steepness |

The `LogisticActivation` class implements a parameterized sigmoid `1/(1 + exp(−η(x − x₀)))` where η controls slope and x₀ controls the midpoint — useful for calibrating output confidence without a separate temperature parameter.

Sources: [get_activation.py](src/models/get_activation.py#L1-L77)

## Configuration-Driven Architecture Variants

All architectural choices are specified through the `projection_layer`, `input_layer`, `num_hid_layers`, and `objective` config tuples — the same Python class instantiates radically different networks. The table below compares the six shipped model configurations:

| Parameter | V6 (Interaction, bin=10) | V6.1 (Interaction, bin=5) | V6.2 (Interaction, full) | V16 (Interface, full) | V16.1 (Interface, bin=5) | V16.2 (Interface, bin=10) |
|-----------|--------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------|------------------------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Objective** | `interaction_bin` | `interaction_bin` | `interaction` | `interface` | `interface_bin` | `interface_bin` |
| **Bin size** | 10 | 5 | 1 | 1 | 5 | 10 |
| **Projection dim** | 128 | 128 | 256 | 128 | 128 | 128 |
| **Projection type** | ln2 | ln2 | ln2 | ln2 | ln2 | ln2 |
| **Interaction ops** | op-od | op-od | op-od | op-od | op-od | op-od |
| **Interface reduce** | — | — | — | avg2d | avg2d | avg2d |
| **Downsample layers** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Upsample layers** | 3 | 3 | 3 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Scale factor** | 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Hidden block** | vanilla | vanilla | vanilla | vanilla | vanilla | vanilla |
| **activation1** | elu | elu | elu | elu | elu | elu |
| **activation2** | sigmoid | sigmoid | sigmoid | sigmoid | sigmoid | sigmoid |

> [!TIP]
> The Version 6.x family and Version 16.x family differ in a fundamental architectural way: V6 models produce **per-pair** predictions (contact maps) by flattening the interaction tensor, while V16 models produce **per-residue** predictions (interface labels) by marginalizing the interaction tensor through avg2d. The hidden bottleneck (upsample=3, scale=2) in V6 expands the 256-d concatenated features through 256→512→1024→2048, whereas V16 skips the hidden block entirely — the avg2d reduction already provides a strong inductive bias for the interface task.

> [!TIP]
> The `state0 → state1 → state2` arithmetic determines the entire feature-width trajectory. For V6 with projection_dim=128: state0=256, state1=256 (0 downsample layers), state2=256×2³=2048 (3 upsample layers). The output linear layer thus maps 2048→1 — a dramatic expansion that gives the final classification ample capacity to disentangle interaction patterns compressed into the 128-d projection.

Sources: [Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.yml](params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.yml#L1-L56), [Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.1.yml](params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.1.yml#L1-L57), [Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.2.yml](params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_6.2.yml#L1-L57), [Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.yml](params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.yml#L1-L56), [Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.1.yml](params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.1.yml#L1-L56), [Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.2.yml](params/Model_config_Epsilon_3_16.2.yml#L1-L56)

## Constructor Parameter Map

The `Epsilon_3.__init__` signature accepts 17 parameters, each mapped from the YAML config via `get_model`. The table below documents every parameter with its config key and role:

| Constructor Param | Config Key | Type | Description |
|-------------------|-----------|------|-------------|
| `emb_size` | `emb_size` | int | Input embedding dimension (1024 for T5) |
| `projection_layer` | `projection_layer` | list | `[dim, type, bias, multiplier, separate]` |
| `output_dim` | `output_dim` | int | Number of output classes (1 for binary) |

| `bias` | `bias` | bool | Whether linear layers include bias |
| `max_len` | `max_seq_len` | int | Maximum padded sequence length |
| `dropouts` | `dropouts` | list | `[proj, residual, upsample, downsample, mc]` rates |
| `norm` | `norm` | list | `[apply_bool, type]` where type ∈ {LN, BN, IN} |
| `temperature` | `temperature` | float/None | Temperature scaling value (None = disabled) |
| `output_layer` | `output_layer` | str | Output layer variant name |
| `objective` | `objective` | list | `[task, bin_size, pool, bin_post_proj, bin_input, single_output]` |
| `device` | `device` | str | Compute device (`cuda` or `cpu`) |

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L16-L20), [get_model.py](src/models/get_model.py#L4-L26)

## Where to Go Next

The Epsilon_3 architecture's interaction tensor is the mathematical heart of the model. To understand the geometric interpretation of the outer-product/outer-difference strategy and why it preserves directional interaction information, see [Projection and Interaction Tensor](6-projection-and-interaction-tensor). For a detailed explanation of how the coarse-grained binning reduces computational cost while preserving predictive accuracy, see [Coarse-Grained Prediction Strategy](7-coarse-grained-prediction-strategy). # Projection and Interaction Tensor



The **Projection and Interaction Tensor** is the architectural core of the Epsilon_3 model — a two-stage computational mechanism that first compresses high-dimensional protein embeddings into a compact latent space, then constructs a 4D tensor encoding pairwise residue-residue relationships between two protein chains. This mechanism is what transforms independent per-chain representations into an interaction-aware joint representation, making it the mathematical bridge between isolated protein understanding and binding prediction.

## Architectural Role and Data Flow

Within the Epsilon_3 forward pass, the projection and interaction tensor stages occupy the first two critical positions in a five-stage pipeline: **Projection → Interaction Tensor → Interface Reduction → Hidden Processing → Output**. The forward method makes this explicit by delegating to `projection_block` and `get_interaction_tensor` sequentially before any downstream processing occurs.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Input
        e1["e₁<br/>(N, L₁, 1024)"]
        e2["e₂<br/>(N, L₂, 1024)"]
    end
    subgraph Projection["Projection Block"]
        P1["projection_layer1<br/>Linear→LN→ELU"]
        P2["projection_layer2<br/>Linear→LN→ELU"]
    end
    subgraph Interaction["Interaction Tensor"]
        Z1["z₁ (N, L₁, d)"]
        Z2["z₂ (N, L₂, d)"]
        OP["op: z₁.unsqueeze(2) × z₂.unsqueeze(1)"]
        OD["od: |z₁.unsqueeze(2) − z₂.unsqueeze(1)|"]
        CAT["Concat → (N, L₁, L₂, 2d)"]
    end
    e1 --> P1 --> Z1
    e2 --> P2 --> Z2
    Z1 --> OP --> CAT
    Z2 --> OD --> CAT
    CAT --> T["Interaction Tensor<br/>(N, L₁, L₂, 2d)"]
```

The interaction tensor **T** ∈ ℝ^{N × L₁ × L₂ × 2d} is the central data structure: each spatial position (i, j) holds a 2d-dimensional feature vector encoding the relationship between residue i of chain 1 and residue j of chain 2. This tensor serves dual purposes depending on the objective — as a full contact map representation for interaction prediction, or as input to a reduction operator for interface prediction.

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L131-L151)

## Projection Block: Dimensionality Compression

The projection block maps raw ProtT5 embeddings from 1024 dimensions to a compact latent space of dimension `projection_dim` (typically 128 or 256). This compression serves both computational efficiency and representational purposes — forcing the model to learn an information bottleneck that retains only interaction-relevant features.

### Shared vs. Separate Projection

The model supports two projection configurations controlled by `projection_layer[4]`. When set to `"separate"`, each chain receives its own independent projection layer (`projection_layer1` and `projection_layer2`), allowing asymmetric feature extraction. When set to `""` (empty string, the default), a **single shared projection layer** is applied to both chains — enforcing weight tying that treats both chains as drawn from the same protein universe, which is the standard configuration across all released model versions.

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L64-L80), [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L155-L178)

### Projection Layer Variants

The `create_projection_layers` factory function produces six normalization-aware variants, each combining a linear transformation with the configured activation (ELU in all released versions). The naming convention follows a positional pattern: the prefix indicates the normalization type (ln/in/bn) and the suffix indicates placement relative to the linear-activation sequence.

| Variant | Architecture | Norm Placement | Notes |
|---------|-------------|----------------|-------|
| `vanilla` | Linear → Activation | None | Baseline, no normalization |
| `ln1` | LayerNorm → Linear → Activation | Pre-linear | Normalizes input features |
| **`ln2`** | **Linear → Activation → LayerNorm** | **Post-activation** | **Default for all released models** |
| `in1` | InstanceNorm1d → Linear → Activation | Pre-linear | Per-sample normalization |
| `in2` | Linear → Activation → InstanceNorm1d | Post-activation | Per-sample normalization |
| `bn1` | BatchNorm1d → Linear → Activation | Pre-linear | Batch-level normalization |
| `bn2` | Linear → Activation → BatchNorm1d | Post-activation | Batch-level normalization |

The `ln2` variant is used universally across all six released configurations (Versions 6, 6.1, 6.2, 16, 16.1, 16.2). Post-activation normalization (suffix `2`) stabilizes the projected representations by normalizing after the nonlinearity has been applied, which prevents feature magnitude drift across training steps — particularly important when the projected embeddings feed directly into outer product operations where uncontrolled magnitudes would compound.

> [!TIP]
> The `in1`/`in2` and `bn1`/`bn2` variants require a `Permute` wrapper to transpose the sequence and feature dimensions before applying 1D normalization, since `InstanceNorm1d` and `BatchNorm1d` expect channel-first format (N, C, L) while the model operates in sequence-first format (N, L, C).

Sources: [get_layers.py](src/models/get_layers.py#L17-L85)

## Interaction Tensor Construction

The `get_interaction_tensor` method is the mechanism that transforms per-chain projected embeddings into a joint interaction space. It operates in two configurable modes determined by `input_layer[1]`.

### Vanilla Mode (`input_layer[1] = "vanilla"`)

This is the default mode used across all released models. The two projection outputs **z₁** ∈ ℝ^{N × L₁ × d} and **z₂** ∈ ℝ^{N × L₂ × d} are independently subjected to two binary interaction operators, then concatenated along the feature dimension:

```
z_i1 = capture_interaction(z1, z2, op1)    →  ℝ^{N × L₁ × L₂ × d}
z_i2 = capture_interaction(z1, z2, op2)    →  ℝ^{N × L₁ × L₂ × d}
interaction_tensor = cat([z_i1, z_i2], dim=-1)  →  ℝ^{N × L₁ × L₂ × 2d}
```

### Concat Mode (`input_layer[1] = "concat"`)

An alternative mode where z₁ and z₂ are first concatenated along the sequence dimension to form z ∈ ℝ^{N × (L₁+L₂) × d}, then both operators are applied to this combined representation against itself. This produces a larger (L₁+L₂) × (L₁+L₂) interaction matrix that includes intra-chain interactions, at significantly higher computational cost.

Sources: [Epsilon_3.py](src/models/Epsilon_3.py#L267-L296)

## Capture Interaction Operators

The `capture_interaction` method implements nine binary operators for combining projected embeddings. These operators fall into three categories based on their output geometry:

### Element-wise Operators (Same-shape outputs)

These require identically-shaped inputs and produce element-wise combinations. They are used for single-position comparisons but **cannot** produce the 4D interaction tensor needed for pairwise residue-residue prediction.

| Operator | Formula | Output Shape | Usage |
|----------|---------|-------------|-------|
| `add` | z₁ + z₂ | (N, L, d) | Element-wise sum |
| `subtract` | z₁ − z₂ | (N, L, d) | Element-wise difference |
| `mag` | \|z₁ − z₂\| | (N, L, d) | Magnitude of difference |
| `multiply` | z₁ ⊙ z₂ | (N, L, d) | Hadamard product |
| `dot` | Σ(z₁ ⊙ z₂) | (N, L, 1) | Scalar dot product |
| `cosine` | cos(z₁, z₂) | (N, L, 1) | Cosine similarity |

### Outer Product Operators (4D tensor outputs)

These are the **primary operators** for interaction tensor construction. They use `unsqueeze` to broadcast the per-chain embeddings into a pairwise comparison space, producing the critical 4D tensor.

| Operator | Formula | Output Shape | Geometric Interpretation |
|----------|---------|-------------|------------------------|
| **`op`** | z₁.unsqueeze(2) ⊙ z₂.unsqueeze(1) | (N, L₁, L₂, d) | **Outer product** — multiplicative interaction at each residue pair |
| **`od`** | \|z₁.unsqueeze(2) − z₂.unsqueeze(1)\| | (N, L₁, L₂, d) | **Outer difference** — distance-based interaction at each residue pair |
| `os` | z₁.unsqueeze(2) + z₂.unsqueeze(1) | (N, L₁, L₂, d) | Outer sum — additive interaction at each residue pair |

### The Default `op-od` Combination

All released models use `input_layer[0] = "op-od"`, combining the outer product and outer difference operators. This pairing captures **complementary geometric information**: the outer product encodes multiplicative feature correlations (which features co-activate across residue pairs), while the outer difference encodes feature-space distances (how dissimilar each residue pair is). Their concatenation yields a 2d-dimensional feature vector per residue pair that is rich in both similarity and dissimilarity signals.

> [!TIP]
> The `op` operator is mathematically equivalent to a bilinear form without learned weights — it computes the Hadamard product of all feature pairs simultaneously.
